name: Opendoor homepage: how the iBuyer prices homes with algorithms
title: Opendoor homepage: how the iBuyer prices homes with algorithms
answer: Opendoor's homepage is the company's own marketing page for its iBuyer service, where homeowners request a cash offer. Its most useful statement for AI watchers is that offers are set using real-time data, advanced pricing algorithms and on-the-ground expertise, analysing comparable sales, current market conditions and the home's features and condition. The page also lists what the final offer includes, including a program fee and a condition adjustment, and says over 310,032 homeowners have been served.

sections.body: Opendoor Labs Inc. publishes this page. It is the company's consumer homepage, a commercial landing page inviting homeowners to request a cash offer for their home rather than list it. Its scope is promotional and practical: it describes the offer process, what a final offer includes, timing, cancellation terms and customer testimonials. No publication or revision date is stated on the page. The text was harvested on 28 September 2026. It is not a technical paper, a filing or a research document, and it contains no methodology detail beyond a short description of how offers are calculated.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page presents Opendoor as a way to sell a home without listing, showings or months of stress, closing on the seller's own timeline. A seller enters an address and a few details and receives an estimated cash offer within 24 hours. After a home assessment, Opendoor sends a final offer within a few days. The final offer is broken into parts: the purchase price for the home, a program fee for selling without staging or showings, a condition adjustment to cover costs of preparing and reselling the home, title and escrow costs of 1 to 3 percent paid to third parties, and the estimated net proceeds after all costs. On pricing, the page says Opendoor uses real-time data, advanced pricing algorithms and on-the-ground expertise. It analyses comparable home sales in the area, current market conditions, and the home's specific features and condition. The page also describes a Cash Now, More Later option, which pairs the convenience of a cash offer with the proceeds of a market transaction. Sellers can cancel any time before closing without cost or penalty by contacting their Customer Experience Partner. The page states that over 310,032 homeowners have been served by Opendoor, and carries three customer testimonials, one noting the offer came in near the appraisal.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: Opendoor states that over 310,032 homeowners have been served. It says an estimated cash offer arrives within 24 hours of entering an address and a few details, and a final offer within a few days after the home assessment. Title and escrow costs are given as 1 to 3 percent, paid to third parties. The final offer is defined as the purchase price plus a program fee, a condition adjustment and title and escrow costs, giving estimated net proceeds after all costs. The page claims offers are set with real-time data, advanced pricing algorithms and on-the-ground expertise, and that sellers can cancel before closing without cost or penalty.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: This is the vendor's own account of how an automated offer is produced, so it is useful as a primary statement of what Opendoor says its pricing algorithms do and what inputs they use: comparable sales, market conditions, and the home's features and condition. For a reader tracking AI in real estate, it shows the consumer-facing side of algorithmic valuation, the point where a model output becomes a cash purchase price with a program fee and condition adjustment attached. It also shows the vocabulary the company uses publicly, which is a starting point for comparing marketing claims against the company's filings and documentation.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Real Estate

sections.body: It is a commercial landing page written to convert visitors into sellers, not an explanation of the models. It gives no detail on model architecture, training data, accuracy, error rates or how the condition adjustment is calculated, and no named methodology. It does not discuss balance-sheet exposure, risk, or how offers perform against resale prices. No author, publication date or version is stated, and the only date attached is the harvest date of 28 September 2026. The figures are self-reported and unaudited on the page. Anyone needing the financial record must go to the company's filings, which this page does not link to or summarise.
